phrases: Nearly two hundred thousand miles from Earth, an oxygen tank on Apollo thirteen blows apart.
Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.
Three astronauts, a dying spaceship, and a lifeboat built for two people for two days.
Here's how duct tape, a slingshot around the Moon, and some brilliant engineering got them home.

chapter: A tank that was already broken

phrases: Apollo was really two spacecraft.
The command and service module, called Odyssey, and the lunar module, called Aquarius.
In the service module sat two oxygen tanks.
They supplied air to breathe, and fed the fuel cells that made the ship's electricity and water.
Oxygen tank two had a hidden history.
Two years earlier, it had been jolted while being removed from another spacecraft.
Then, in a ground test, it wouldn't empty properly.
So technicians switched on its internal heater, for hours, to boil the oxygen off.
The heater's safety switches were rated for twenty-eight volts.
But the ground power supply ran at sixty-five.
The switches welded shut.
Inside the tank, temperatures reached over five hundred degrees Celsius, and cooked the insulation on the wires.
Fifty-six hours into the flight, Mission Control asked for a routine stir of the oxygen tanks, switching on small fans inside.
The damaged wires sparked, and the insulation caught fire, inside a tank full of pure oxygen.
The pressure soared, the tank failed, and the blast blew a whole panel off the side of the service module.
Both tanks lost their oxygen.
The fuel cells died, one by one.
Odyssey was running out of power.
The Moon landing was off.
Now the only goal was getting home alive.
The crew moved into the lunar module, Aquarius, and shut Odyssey down, to save its batteries for re-entry.
Aquarius was built to keep two people alive for about two days.
Now it had to keep three alive for about four.
Power, water and heat were cut to the bone.
The cabin dropped to just a few degrees above freezing.

chapter: A square filter in a round hole

phrases: But a new danger was building.
Carbon dioxide, from three people breathing.
Canisters of lithium hydroxide scrub it out of the air.
Aquarius had round ones, and they were filling up.
Odyssey had plenty of spares.
But they were square, and they wouldn't fit the lunar module's round sockets.
On the ground, engineers raced to build an adapter, using only things the crew had on board.
Plastic bags.
Cardboard from the flight plan.
A spacesuit hose.
A sock.
And lots of duct tape.
The crew built it from instructions read up over the radio.
And the carbon dioxide level started to fall.
To get home, they needed the Moon's gravity.
But Apollo thirteen had left its safe, free-return path, to aim for its landing site.
So they fired Aquarius's descent engine, built to land on the Moon, to put them back on a path that would swing around the Moon and fall back toward Earth.
Behind the Moon, they flew farther from Earth than any humans had ever been.
After the Moon, another burn sped them up, to get home sooner.
Near Earth, they let the service module go, and saw the damage for the first time.
A whole side was missing.
They brought the frozen Odyssey back to life, using a power-up plan worked out on the ground.
Then they let go of Aquarius, the lifeboat that had saved them.
On April the seventeenth, nineteen seventy, Odyssey splashed down in the Pacific.
All three astronauts were safe.
NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks.
No fans inside, wiring sheathed in stainless steel, and a third tank in a separate bay.
An extra battery was added to the service module too.
A jolted tank, the wrong voltage and one routine stir nearly killed them.
Duct tape, a slingshot and thousands of engineers brought them home.
Could you have built that filter, with only what was on board?
